example.problem: You borrow $35,000 for college at 5.5% annual interest and repay it over 10 years. What is the monthly payment, and how much interest do you pay in total?
example.title: A 10-year student loan

faqs.a: Use the formula with your numbers, or this calculator. For example, $35,000 at 5.5% over 10 years gives about $379.84 per month in principal and interest.
faqs.q: How do I calculate my monthly student loan payment?

faqs.a: It lowers the monthly payment but raises the total interest a lot. Borrowing the same $35,000 at 5.5% over 20 years instead of 10 drops the payment to about $240.70 but raises total interest from $10,581 to about $22,768.
faqs.q: What happens if I stretch repayment over more years?

faqs.a: It is exactly the same idea, but student loans often have smaller balances, shorter terms, and no property as collateral, so rates are usually higher than mortgage rates. Both use the same amortization formula.
faqs.q: Is a student loan payment calculated like a mortgage payment?

faqs.a: Yes, usually without a penalty on federal loans and most private loans. Paying extra goes straight to the principal, which cuts the total interest. Even $50 extra a month on the example above saves about $1,900 in interest and ends the loan a year early.
faqs.q: Can I pay extra to finish a student loan early?

formula.label: Monthly payment
formula.note: P is the loan amount, r the monthly rate, n the number of payments

formula.label: Total interest
formula.note: What you pay overall minus what you borrowed

howItWorks: A student loan is repaid in equal monthly installments that cover both interest and principal. The calculator first converts your annual rate to a monthly rate and your years to a number of payments, then applies the standard amortization formula: payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n). Because interest is charged on the remaining balance each month, early payments are mostly interest and later payments are mostly principal.

This is an estimate for planning purposes, not financial advice. Real student loans may have fees, variable rates, or income-based repayment options, and federal loans have protections private loans do not. Always read the loan terms and confirm figures with your lender or financial aid office before borrowing.

When you compare loan offers, look past the monthly payment. Two loans with the same payment can have very different total interest if their rates or terms differ, so always compare the total interest line as well. And if you can afford even a small extra payment each month, put it toward the principal: on a typical 10-year loan, $50 extra a month cuts more than a year off the term and saves well over a thousand dollars in interest.

mistakes.text: The formula divides by the monthly rate (annual ÷ 12). Using 5.5 directly instead of 0.0045833 makes the payment impossibly large.
mistakes.title: Forgetting to convert the annual rate to a monthly rate

mistakes.text: Ten years means 120 payments, not 10. Forgetting the ×12 step makes the answer roughly twelve times too big.
mistakes.title: Using years instead of number of payments

mistakes.text: Lenders quote annual rates, but interest accrues monthly. A '5.5% loan' costs you 0.45833% of the remaining balance every month, not 5.5% of the original amount each year.
mistakes.title: Treating the annual rate as if it were charged once a year

mistakes.text: Doubling the term from 10 to 20 years more than doubles the total interest, because you pay interest for twice as long on a balance that shrinks slowly. Always compare total interest, not just the monthly payment.
mistakes.title: Comparing loans by monthly payment alone
